subject: language_arts

unit.title: Apostrophes & homophones
unit.essentialQuestion: When does a word need an apostrophe, and how do I pick between sound-alike words?

title: Homophones: to / too / two & friends (retrieval)
objectives: By the end, I can choose the right homophone from sound-alike sets by meaning.

vocabulary.definition: the number 2 — it has the w, like its cousins twin and twice
also or very — the EXTRA o for 'extra'
vocabulary.example: Can I come too? It's too hot!

vocabulary.definition: the everyday one for everything else
here = this place; hear = with your ears (ear is inside it!)
vocabulary.example: Come here. Did you hear that?

vocabulary.definition: see = with your eyes; sea = the water

emphasize: Choose sound-alikes by MEANING — always name the meaning before choosing.
The tricks: two has the w (twin, twice); too has an EXTRA o for 'extra'; to is the everyday one for everything else; hear has ear inside.
This is a retrieval lesson: interleave the whole unit — there/their/they're AND both apostrophe jobs AND the plural trap.

keyConcepts: two = number, too = also/very, to = everything else
spaced retrieval of there/their/they're and apostrophe rules
misconceptions: defaulting to plain to for every gap
missing the extra o when the meaning is 'also' or 'very'
unit slips creeping back: there/their swaps, plural apostrophes (egg's), it's/its
hooks: 'Two biscuits is too many to eat!' — three sound-alikes in ONE sentence. Untangle them and you've mastered the whole unit.

digital: cue cards on screen (two = number / too = also or very / to = the rest; here/hear, see/sea)

plan.goal: The tongue-twister sentence sets the challenge; quick spaced retrieval of yesterday's set.
plan.note: Read the sentence aloud so all three sound identical. Retrieval question before any new teaching.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers they're for the warm-up and hears that the three new words sound the same.

script.say: Here's a tongue-twister of a sentence: 'Two biscuits is too many to eat!' Three sound-alikes in ONE sentence — and they all sound like 'too'! By the end you'll untangle them every time. First, a quick warm-up on yesterday's three. Which one means 'they are'?
script.adaptHints: Listen for they're. If shaky, quick recall: there (place), their (belonging), they're (they are) — then move on; the bank will bring them back.

stuckProtocol: If they're won't come: stretch it out loud — 'THEY ARE' — and show the apostrophe standing in for the missing a.

plan.goal: Teach the two/too/to meanings with their tricks, plus the here/hear and see/sea pairs.
plan.note: Circle the w of two, the extra o of too, the ear inside hear. Keep it brisk — this is a review lesson.
plan.successCriteria: Child can say: two = number, too = also/very (extra o for extra), to = everything else; hear has ear inside.

script.say: Three more sound-alikes, all chosen by meaning. Two — that's the NUMBER, 2. It's got that w, like its cousins twin and twice. Too — means ALSO or VERY: 'me too', 'too hot'. Here's the trick: it has an EXTRA o — an extra o for 'extra'! To — is the everyday one for everything else: 'I'm going to school'. And two more pairs: here, this place — hear, with your ears, and look — ear is hiding inside it! See, with your eyes — sea, the water.
script.adaptHints: Make the 'extra o for extra' trick a chant. Point at each circled clue as you say it.

rows: the w — like twin and twice
blocks.caption: Name the meaning first — then choose the spelling.

plan.goal: Shared choices naming the meaning first: 'I have ___ cats' (two) and 'Can I come ___?' (too), plus one hear example.
plan.note: Meaning named aloud before every choice — that's the routine the whole practice runs on.
plan.successCriteria: Child fills both gaps correctly, naming the meaning first.

script.say: Choose with me. 'I have ___ cats.' How many — is it a number? Yes! So it's two, the one with the w. Now yours: 'Can I come ___?' — it means 'also', so which one? Remember the trick… the extra o for extra! And one more: 'Did you ___ that noise?' — with your ears — which spelling has an ear hiding inside?
script.adaptHints: If the child answers without naming the meaning, replay: 'meaning first, then choose.' Swap cats for the child's favourite animal.

wrongAnswers.why: picked the everyday one without naming the meaning
wrongAnswers.remedy: Does it mean 'also' here? Yes — so it needs the extra o: too.
Is it a number, 2? No — it means 'also'. That's too, the extra-o one.

plan.goal: Diagnostic: the 'also' gap — too with its trick named.
plan.note: Probe after a correct answer: 'what's the memory trick?' (extra o for extra).
plan.successCriteria: Child picks too and states the extra-o trick.

script.say: Quick exam: 'I want to come ___.' — the missing word means 'also'. Which spelling — and what's the memory trick?
script.adaptHints: Listen for too + 'extra o for extra'. Celebrate the trick as their tool for life.

blocks.explain: It means 'also', so it takes the extra o — too. Extra o for extra!

check.question: 'I want to come ___.' — the word that means 'also'.

wrongAnswers.why: the everyday one grabbed by default
wrongAnswers.remedy: Does it mean 'also' here? Yes — so it needs the extra o: too.
Is it a number, 2? No — it means 'also'. That's too, the extra-o one.

plan.goal: Interleaved retrieval: mixed gaps across to/too/two, here/hear, see/sea, there/their/they're AND apostrophe items from the whole unit.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2 — deliberately interleave: never two items on the same skill in a row. This is the unit's spaced-review engine.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 4+ of 6 mixed items correctly, naming the meaning (or the apostrophe question) aloud first.

script.say: Grand unit challenge! Everything from this whole unit is in the mix — sound-alikes, squashed words, belonging, and fake apostrophes. For every one: say the meaning or ask the apostrophe question FIRST, then answer. Show me the expert you've become!
script.adaptHints: Rotate skills so no two consecutive items match. Theme sentences with the learner's interests; never change the target words.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'let's say the meaning first.'
Step down: show the meaning cue cards; offer two choices.
ONE hint: 'is it a number? does it mean also? if not, it's plain to.'
Keep it safe: 'These trip up everyone — naming the meaning is your superpower.'

plan.goal: Child teaches back the three 'too'-sounding words and how to pick; end the unit on a win.
plan.note: Child-led. Close the unit warmly — this trick is theirs for life.
plan.successCriteria: Child states: two = number, too = also/very (extra o), to = everything else; choose by meaning.

script.say: Tell me the three 'too'-sounding words and how you pick. … Exactly: two is the number, too means also or very — extra o for extra — and to is the everyday one. You named the meaning before every choice — that's exactly how to untangle sound-alikes. The 'extra o for extra' trick is yours forever now. And that's the whole unit: squashing, belonging, no fake apostrophes, and sound-alikes sorted by meaning. What a set of tools!
script.adaptHints: Recap the unit's four tools by name. End with specific process praise for today's meaning-first habit.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Meaning first: is it a number here? Yes, 2! Which spelling is the number — the one with the w, like twin?

wrongAnswers.why: grabbed the extra-o one without checking the meaning
wrongAnswers.remedy: Does it mean 'also' or 'very'? No — it's counting shoes. The number one has the w.

hints: How many shoes — is the gap a number?
The number 2 is the one with the w: two, like twin and twice.

reteach.say: Counting? Then it's two, the number — with the w it shares with twin and twice. One, two shoes. Number = two, every time.

block.caption: two shoes — the number with the w

wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Me too!' means 'me ALSO!' — also gets the extra o for extra.
Is anyone counting to 2 here? No — it means 'also'. Extra o for extra!

hints: What does 'Me ___!' mean — me ALSO!
Also = the extra o.

reteach.say: 'Me too!' is the friendliest 'also' there is. Also or very always take the extra o — an extra o for something extra. Me tooooo!

block.caption: me too = me ALSO — extra o for extra

wrongAnswers.why: the extra o added where nothing is 'extra'
wrongAnswers.remedy: Does it mean 'also' or 'very'? No — it's just going somewhere. Not a number, not also — so it's plain to.
Is 2 of anything being counted? No — it's the everyday going-somewhere word: to.

hints: Run the checks: a number? means also/very?
Neither — so it's the everyday one: to.

reteach.say: The plain to is the everyday worker: going TO school, giving TO a friend. Check the two specials first — not a number, not 'also/very'? Then plain to wins.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Is it about a place, or about your EARS? Listening needs the spelling with an ear hiding inside: hear.
Find the whole word ear and keep it together: h-EAR.

hints: Is it a place, or something you do with your ears?
The ears one has ear inside: h-ear.

reteach.say: You HEAR with your EAR — and the word hear keeps a whole ear inside it! Here without the a is the place, like its cousin there. Noise? Ears? hear.

wrongAnswers.why: eyes word chosen for the water
wrongAnswers.remedy: Are we looking at something, or swimming in the WATER? The water is the sea.
Say the sentence again slowly — we swam in the… water word: sea.

hints: Is it about eyes, or about water?
Swimming happens in the water one: sea.

reteach.say: Two spellings: see with double e is your EYES — I see you! Sea with e-a is the big blue WATER. We swam in the water, so it's sea. You can even SEE the SEA — both in one sentence!

block.caption: see with your eyes — swim in the sea

wrongAnswers.remedy: Whose kite is it? It belongs to the twins — which word has the owner, heir, hiding inside?
Run yesterday's test: 'the twins lost they are kite'? Nonsense — it's belonging.

hints: Yesterday's set! Whose kite is it?
Belonging = the one with heir inside.

reteach.say: Yesterday's experts don't rust! Three questions: say 'they are'? — no. A place? — no. Belongs to them? — YES. The kite is theirs: their, with heir the owner hiding inside.

block.explain: The o of not drops out and the apostrophe stands in its place: don't.

wrongAnswers.why: the gravestone forgotten after a few days
wrongAnswers.remedy: A letter went missing when we squashed — which one? Mark its gap.
The apostrophe sits exactly where the o of not dropped — between the n and the t.

hints: Squash do and not — which letter falls out?
The apostrophe is the o's gravestone: don't.

reteach.say: Back to Job 1: do not → squash → the o of not falls out → don't. Find the missing letters, bury them with the apostrophe — same move as ever.

block.caption: don't — the ' buried where the o was

block.statement: The shop sign 'fresh egg's for sale' is written correctly.
block.explain: False! Nothing belongs and no letters are missing — plain plural: fresh eggs. Plurals never take an apostrophe.

wrongAnswers.remedy: Inspector question: do the eggs OWN anything? Are letters missing? No and no — cross that apostrophe out.

wrongAnswers.why: swapped one wrong apostrophe for another
wrongAnswers.remedy: No apostrophe anywhere — it's just more than one egg: eggs.

hints: Put your inspector badge back on: belonging? missing letters?
Neither — so what does a plain plural get?

reteach.say: Once an inspector, always an inspector! Fresh egg's — do the eggs own anything? No. Letters missing? No. Just more than one egg — fresh eggs, no apostrophe. Fakes never sneak past you.

practiceBank.skill: interleave the whole unit: sort apostrophe jobs vs plurals

block.prompt: Grand unit sort! Put each one in the right pile.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: can't + they're → squashing; Sam's bag + Gran's hat → belonging; two dogs + three buses → plural

wrongAnswers.why: the s pulling towards the apostrophe piles again
wrongAnswers.remedy: Do the dogs own anything? Are letters missing? No — 'more than one' has its own no-apostrophe pile.
Stretch it: they're = THEY ARE — letters went missing, so it's a squash. The belonging one is t-h-e-i-r.

hints: One question per card: belonging? missing letters? neither?
they're stretches to 'they are' — what does that make it?

reteach.say: The whole unit in one sort! Squashes stretch back out (can't = can not, they're = they are). Belongings have an owner (Sam, Gran). Plurals just mean more — and get nothing at all. Ask the question, place the card.

practiceBank.skill: choose too and to in one sentence

block.prompt: It is ___ hot ___ play outside. Which pair fills the gaps?
block.explain: 'VERY hot' → too (extra o); 'to play' is the everyday to.

wrongAnswers.why: the pair reversed — meanings not checked per gap
wrongAnswers.remedy: Gap one means VERY hot — very takes the extra o. Gap two is the everyday 'to play'.
Is anything being counted? No — 'very hot' wants the extra o: too.

hints: Do each gap separately: does it mean very? is it a number?
Very = extra o; the everyday one goes with 'play'.

reteach.say: Two gaps, two checks. 'It is ___ hot' — that's VERY hot — extra o: too. '___ play outside' — not a number, not 'also' — plain everyday to. Meaning first, gap by gap.

practiceBank.skill: write two, too and to in one sentence

block.prompt: Write one sentence that uses two, too AND to — like the biscuit one!
block.sample: Two biscuits is too many to eat!

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: A sentence using two (number), too (also/very) and to (everyday) each correctly

wrongAnswers.answer: a sentence with the spellings swapped
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it back gap by gap: point at your number, your 'also/very', and your everyday one. Fix any word doing the wrong job.

wrongAnswers.answer: a sentence using only one or two of them
wrongAnswers.remedy: Start from a number of things — 'Two…' — then make them 'too' something, then add a 'to'. Copy the biscuit shape!

hints: Borrow the shape: [Two things] is too [something] to [do].
Say it aloud first, then write it.

reteach.say: Use the biscuit sentence as a recipe: pick TWO of something you love… say they're TOO much of something… TO do something. 'Two puppies is too wriggly to hold!' Your turn — say it, then write it.

block.caption: Two … too … to — the recipe sentence

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, force full interleaving — rotate to/too/two, other pairs, there/their/they're and apostrophe items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach with the meaning cue cards shown, then a level-1 item on that same skill before mixing again.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 5+ correct across the mix including at least one to/too/two, one there/their/they're retrieval and one apostrophe retrieval → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'homophones by meaning' and unit-3 retention confirmed.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'let's say the meaning first.'
Step down: meaning prompt cards; two choices per gap.
ONE hint: 'is it a number? does it mean also? if not, it's plain to.'
Keep it safe: 'These trip up everyone — naming the meaning is your superpower.'
adaptivity.personalization: Theme gaps around the learner's favourites ('Two dinosaurs is too many to fit in the bath!'). The meaning-first habit stays in every framing.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable gap; praise the process — 'you named the meaning before every choice, all unit long.'

differentiation.support: Meaning prompts stay on each word; two choices per gap; the tutor reads the sentence and names the meaning together with the child.
differentiation.stretch: Explain the 'too = extra o' trick in their own words and write a sentence using two, too and to correctly.

extension: Spot here/hear or see/sea in a favourite book and explain which is which.
assessmentEvidence: Child chooses correctly in at least four of six mixed gaps, states the too = extra o trick, and answers the apostrophe retrievals (contraction + plural trap).
revisitLater: End-of-Unit 3 check — can't, Sam's bag, dogs (no apostrophe), and They're/their/there. Re-pose one to/too/two gap as a quick retrieval in Unit 4.
